source.title: Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight
source.authors: Shashwat Goel; Joschka Strüber; I. Auzina; Karuna K Chandra; P. Kumaraguru; D. Kiela; Ameya Prabhu; Matthias Bethge; Jonas Geiping

page_placements.theme: What the student takes from the supervisor: error imitation, pseudo-label correction, coverage expansion, complementary knowledge, style
Weak supervision beating strong training on gold or on the same labels (PGR above 1, OPR above 1)

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It applies weak-to-strong training to open-weight models and tests whether similarity predicts training gains, but reports gain over the initial student rather than Burns et al.'s PGR measure.
record.gate_note: Section 4 directly tests weak-to-strong training and its relationship to model similarity. It does not calculate PGR. The confidence-weighted loss is used as the training recipe, not compared against alternative training changes. Referenced findings from other papers are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: It runs Burns et al.'s weak-to-strong setup: the same confidence-weighted loss and 15 of the same binary NLP tasks, on 12 newer open-weight model pairs. It reports the trained student against the weak supervisor, and how weak–strong error similarity predicts the gain. The measure differs from the original: the gain is over the initial strong student, not PGR. That makes it T2 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the student surpasses the supervisor but stays below the ground-truth elicitation ceiling. They find similarity between supervisor and student predicts the gain in advance, with less similar pairs gaining more. They attribute part of the gain to complementary knowledge beyond elicitation, and propose a higher ceiling. They state that the relationship is correlational and that causation is not established.
record.recipe_differences: Follows the Burns et al. weak-to-strong setup and uses its confidence-weighted fine-tuning objective, but studies newer open-weight models and reports gain relative to the initial student rather than PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The relationship between CAPA similarity and gain varies across tasks and weak–strong model pairs; the paper reports different negative correlations for the 12 pairs.

fits_no_version.finding: On test samples where the supervisor was wrong but the ground-truth-elicited student was right, the weak-to-strong student is correct 71.9% of the time. Where the supervisor was right and the elicited student wrong, it is correct 42.2% of the time. On the training split the two quadrants are roughly equal (0.56 vs 0.59).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-to-strong gains come partly from transfer of the weak supervisor's complementary knowledge, beyond eliciting the strong model's latent knowledge.

fits_no_version.finding: A ceiling built from the union of supervisor and elicited-model correct answers gives +14.1 over the initial student, against +11.2 for the elicited model alone.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The strong-on-ground-truth ceiling underestimates the gains achievable from weak supervision.

record.problems: PGR is not reported, and the authors use a different gain measure. Experiments cover 15 binary NLP tasks and 12 selected model pairs. The paper says it discarded three additional weak models after some produced negative gains and excluded Hellaswag because model accuracies were low.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Table 11 reports per-pair test accuracies for four correctness quadrants, and Table 12 reports corresponding training-set values; these detailed decompositions are not separately rowed here because the paper's main text reports aggregate quadrant results (R16–R17). Appendix Figure 16 also reports correlations using alternative similarity metrics.

untested.parts: PGR as Burns defines it is not computed. The elicited ceiling is trained on Dtr1, not Dtr2.
Not tested. The confidence loss is used throughout, with no comparison against naive fine-tuning or other methods.
Not tested: chess, reward modelling, systematic scaling of supervisor or student size, representation-level predictors, and any causal test of similarity.
Not tested: students exploiting what the supervisor cannot check, and distribution shift.

missing.what: Per-dataset test accuracies of weak supervisor, initial student, weak-to-strong student and ceilings. The text says the student beats the supervisor on all 15 datasets; per-dataset V1 rows are needed.

Discarded weak supervisors (SmolLM 1.7B, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Llama-3.2-1B). Their accuracy was below the initial strong student, and weak-to-strong training lowered the student's accuracy on some tasks. No numbers are given.

record.verdict_notes: Results were selected: weak models whose supervision gave negative gains were dropped, which may inflate V1 support and the similarity correlation. Table 9 lists Llama-3.2-1B as a weak model, but the results use Llama-3.2-3B and the text says Llama-3.2-1B was discarded. This is an internal inconsistency. Similarity varies mostly by task rather than by model pair, so the V3/V4 correlations are largely across tasks. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: PGR is not calculated; the paper reports accuracy gains relative to the initial strong student instead.
No comparison of auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling supervisors, or alternative loss variants.

The study tests four weak and three strong open-weight models on 15 binary NLP tasks and examines similarity as a predictor. It does not test chess, reward modelling, or representation-level predictors, and does not isolate a causal effect of model size.
It tests whether gains vary with weak–strong similarity, but not exploitation of supervisor-checking limits or distribution shift.
No theory establishing conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.
No vision experiment; vision work is mentioned as related work.

rows.size_stated: 4 weak models in the 1–3B range; 3 strong models in the 7–9B range
rows.stage_stated: pretrained models; task-finetuned for the experiment
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune strong students on weak-supervisor annotations using the confidence-weighted objective.

conditions.value: 180 training runs; average across 15 datasets and 12 model pairs

rows.measure: Accuracy and accuracy gain relative to initial strong student
rows.baseline: Initial Strong Student: 75.1%; Weak Supervisor: +4.1 accuracy gap relative to the initial student
rows.value: Weak to Strong Trained Student: +7.4 accuracy gap relative to the initial student. The text also states that the trained student surpasses the weak supervisor across datasets.
rows.note: The reported gains are not PGR. The table gives gains relative to the initial strong student; no PGR value is provided.
rows.check: State and link are correct. The weak-to-strong student is +7.4 against the supervisor's +4.1, both relative to the initial student. That is about 3.3 points above the supervisor, and Fig. 17 says it surpasses the supervisor on every dataset. An approximate PGR is (7.4−4.1)/(11.2−4.1) ≈ 0.46, but the paper's elicited ceiling is trained on Dtr1, not Dtr2, so this is not Burns's PGR.

source_check.problem: The included analysis excludes additional weak supervisors whose training produced negative gains, as disclosed in Appendix C.1.

tranche.reason: Tests the same weak-to-strong question using open-weight models, LoRA and a gain-over-initial-student measure rather than the original PGR measure.

statements.correction: Three strong students: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, gemma-2-9b; four weak supervisors; 12 pairs; 15 tasks; aggregate r = −0.85; accuracy-gap-controlled partial r = −0.35; causal effects not established.

statements.problem: The no-code assertion is unresolved from the supplied text. The theme assignment about weak supervision beating gold training overstates a proposed union ceiling; this study's trained student remains below its elicited model.
